blocks.text: A standard Fenwick tree natively supports point update plus range query, changing one element and querying a sum over a range. But real problems sometimes need the OPPOSITE combination, or even BOTH range updates and range queries together. This topic covers the four possible combinations and the specific techniques that unlock the harder ones.
There is no single "one size fits all" Fenwick tree. Choosing the right technique starts with correctly identifying which of the four update/query combinations a problem actually needs.

blocks.caption: The four combinations of update type and query type, from trivial to genuinely advanced.

items: Point update, point query: trivial, does not even need a Fenwick tree, a plain array suffices.
Point update, range query: the standard configuration, covered in the sibling point-update and prefix-sum-query topics.
Range update, point query: a genuinely different technique using a Fenwick tree over DIFFERENCES rather than raw values.
Range update, range query: the hardest combination, requiring TWO Fenwick trees working together.

content.title: 2. Range Update, Point Query: The Difference Trick

blocks.text: Maintain a Fenwick tree over the DIFFERENCE array, where diff[i] equals arr[i] minus arr[i-1]. To add a delta to every element in range [l, r], only TWO point updates are needed on the difference tree: add delta at position l, subtract delta at position r+1.

blocks.caption: A range update becomes just two point updates on the difference array: add delta at the start of the range, subtract it right after the range ends.
blocks.alt: Range Update, Point Query: The Difference Trick

blocks.text: This works because of the prefix sum identity: querying the prefix sum of the difference array UP TO index i reconstructs arr[i] exactly. Adding delta at l and subtracting it at r+1 means every index from l through r accumulates the extra delta when the prefix sum is taken, while indices before l or after r cancel it out exactly, the addition and subtraction fall outside their prefix sum range.

Applying a range update of add 5 to indices 2 through 4 on a difference array: perform update(2, +5) and update(5, -5) on the difference tree (5 = r+1 = 4+1). A point query at index 3 (inside the range) now returns the original value plus 5, since the prefix sum up to index 3 includes the +5 added at position 2 and has not yet reached the -5 at position 5. A point query at index 6 (outside the range) returns the original value unchanged, since both the +5 and the -5 are included in its prefix sum and cancel out exactly.

content.title: 4. Range Update, Range Query: The Dual Tree Technique

blocks.text: The single difference tree above only supports POINT query correctly, not range query, because summing the reconstructed point values across a range requires accounting for how many times each update's delta effectively contributes to each position, which the single tree does not track.

The standard fix maintains TWO Fenwick trees: B1, identical to the difference tree above, and a second auxiliary tree B2 that tracks a correction term. The prefix sum formula becomes prefixSum(i) equals i times B1.query(i) minus B2.query(i), where B2 is updated with delta times (l-1) at position l and negative delta times r at position r+1 during a range update.

This is a genuinely more advanced derivation. The core intuition: B1 alone would overcount or undercount depending on WHERE within the range a given index falls, and the "i times B1.query(i)" term combined with B2's correction exactly compensates for that position dependent effect, restoring a correct range sum.

content.title: 5. C++ Implementation: Range Update, Point Query

blocks.text: Both the range update / point query variant and the range update / range query variant run in O(log n) per operation, the same bound as a basic Fenwick tree. This is achieved by cleverly reformulating what is stored (differences instead of raw values, plus a correction tree for the range query case), not by any fundamentally new asymptotic technique.

blocks.text: Forgetting the r+1 subtraction when doing a range update on the difference tree: without it, the added delta would incorrectly extend past the intended range forever, since nothing cancels it out.

Confusing which combination a given problem actually needs and reaching for the wrong technique, always identify whether updates are point or range, and whether queries are point or range, BEFORE choosing an implementation.
Mixing up when to use "i times B1.query(i)" versus just B1.query(i) directly: the correction term is only needed for the range query variant, using it for a plain point query produces a wrong result.

Range Sum Query Mutable is combination 2. Range Addition covers combination 3, range update plus point query. Combination 4, full range update range query, is a genuinely advanced competitive programming technique, less commonly required in typical interviews but valuable to know exists.
